evidence_quote: the “totality of the circumstances” inquiry has no time limit
independent: isolated manifest; no sibling votes or adjudications disclosed
reasons: The Court's Held expressly states the excessive-force inquiry requires objective reasonableness from 'the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene' and demands analyzing the 'totality of the circumstances' (Graham, Mendez, Garner cited), which faithfully tracks the proposition's first clause.
The opinion states in terms that the totality inquiry 'has no time limit' and that no rule precluding consideration of prior events is reconcilable with the fact-dependent approach.
The Court squarely rejects the moment-of-threat rule: 'Today, we reject that approach as improperly narrowing the requisite Fourth Amendment analysis'.
The proposition does not overclaim: it does not assert anything about the reserved officer-created-danger question, which the opinion explicitly declined to decide.
residual_risks: The holding is expressly limited to force used 'during a stop or arrest'.
The opinion notes the situation at the precise moment 'will often matter most'.

evidence_quote: the police may also examine the contents of any containers found within the passenger compartment
independent: isolated manifest; no sibling votes or adjudications disclosed
reasons: The holding language matches the proposition's first clause: 'when a policeman has made a lawful custodial arrest of the occupant of an automobile, he may, as a contemporaneous incident of that arrest, search the passenger compartment of that automobile.'
The container clause is directly supported: 'the police may also examine the contents of any containers found within the passenger compartment.'
The opinion ties the container authority to the arrest and defines 'container' broadly (footnote 4).
The proposition correctly limits itself to the passenger compartment; footnote 4 confirms the holding 'does not encompass the trunk'.
residual_risks: The opinion also covers a 'recent occupant,' which the proposition compresses to 'occupant'; this narrows rather than overstates.
Belton's contemporaneity requirement (later narrowed by Gant/Thornton) is captured by 'contemporaneously'.

evidence_quote: the police officer must be able to point to specific and articulable facts which, taken together with rational inferences from those facts, reasonably warrant that intrusion
independent: isolated manifest; no sibling votes or adjudications disclosed
reasons: The 'reasonable, articulable suspicion grounded in specific facts and rational inferences' standard is verbatim Terry.
The 'not probable cause' clause is supported: 'a narrowly drawn authority to permit a reasonable search for weapons ... regardless of whether he has probable cause to arrest.'
QUALIFICATION: Terry's operative holding is about the protective frisk keyed to 'armed and presently dangerous' — not a general reasonable-suspicion standard for the investigative stop as such.

The opinion expressly reserves the investigative-stop standard in footnote 16: 'We thus decide nothing today concerning the constitutional propriety of an investigative seizure upon less than probable cause for purposes of detention and/or interrogation.' Attributing a settled stop-standard holding to Terry overstates what this opinion decided.
residual_risks: A fully 'refuted' call would wrongly discard a widely accurate black-letter summary; an unqualified 'stands' would credit Terry with deciding the stop standard it expressly reserved.
The frisk standard (armed-and-dangerous) is narrower than generic 'reasonable suspicion of criminal activity'.
suggested_tightening: Attribute the frisk standard to Terry's holding and note that Terry supplied the specific-and-articulable-facts standard while expressly reserving the investigative-stop/detention standard (fn. 16), later settled in subsequent cases.

evidence_quote: We therefore decline to extend Robinson to searches of data on cell phones, and hold instead that officers must generally secure a warrant before conducting such a search.
independent: isolated manifest; no sibling votes or adjudications disclosed
reasons: The opinion holds exactly the non-extension of Robinson: 'We therefore decline to extend Robinson to searches of data on cell phones, and hold instead that officers must generally secure a warrant before conducting such a search.'
The syllabus Held confirms the warrant requirement.
The proposition correctly uses the hedge 'generally,' matching the Court's own qualifier.
'Robinson bright-line' is accurate: the opinion characterizes Robinson's 'categorical rule' as the rule it declines to extend.
residual_risks: The word 'generally' is load-bearing — exigent circumstances remain available. The proposition preserves this hedge.
The holding concerns digital contents, not the physical phone; the proposition's framing is precise.

evidence_quote: the “automobile exception” has no separate exigency requirement
independent: isolated manifest; no sibling votes or adjudications disclosed
reasons: The opinion states the rule verbatim: 'the automobile exception has no separate exigency requirement.'
The readily-mobile/probable-cause formulation is quoted from Labron.
The 'even with ample time to obtain one' clause is grounded in the disposition: the Court reversed a holding premised on there being no exigency preventing a warrant.
The Court holds the 'abundant probable cause' finding 'alone satisfies the automobile exception.'
residual_risks: The 'readily mobile' predicate is stated but was not contested here; the proposition retains it.
This is a per curiam summary reversal restating Ross/Labron rather than announcing new law.
